transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Delaire (Redwood SE), June Park (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (VelaHealth), Ethan Cole (VelaHealth), Sara Ortiz (VelaHealth), Marta Lin (VelaHealth)

[00:00:05] Alyssa: okay good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, uh let's kick off the metadata driven prefetch sync. quick agenda, recap of last week's numbers, what we changed, hit rates, latency impact, then action items. Marcus do you want to start with the metrics?

[00:00:28] Marcus: yeah sure, so last week we flipped the initial prefetch prototype, the one that looks up entity tags from the session metadata and primes the KV for likely prefixes. baseline hit rate across the test cohort was about 12% for prefix hits, with the proto we saw it up to 28% median across the cohort but there's high variance, um like certain cohorts were 5% and some 45% so it's pretty workload dependent. p95 latency increased by about 15 milliseconds because of the extra prefetch lookups but token generator p50 stayed the same.

[00:01:05] Priya: can I pause, sorry, that variance is my main worry — the marketing cohort is very chatty with short queries so their prefix reuse is low, whereas the clinician notes cohort reuses a lot. is there a way to make the prefetch more selective? we don't want to waste cycles warming caches that don't help.

[00:01:28] Marcus: absolutely, that was the point of v2 we've been working on — metadata-driven scoring. instead of prefetching every potential key we score candidate prefixes using a lightweight heuristic model (session type, last-turn tokens, metadata tags) and only prefetch above a threshold. in staging that bumped the effective hit rate for cohorts that benefited while drastically reducing wasted prefetches — overall CPU for prefetching dropped by ~40%.

[00:01:55] Sara: sorry can you explain the heuristic model? is it a learned model or a ruleset?

[00:02:01] Marcus: it's hybrid, so right now it's rules with a small trained classifier we call the "prefetch scorer" that looks at frequency and recency and a couple of categorical signals from your metadata. the classifier is trained on historical session traces you provided last quarter, but we keep the threshold tunable per-cohort.

[00:02:20] Marta: one question — how are you representing metadata? do we need to change our payloads?

[00:02:25] June: good point. currently we accept a small metadata block in the request header — key names you already send: user_type, session_intent, content_tags. we map those into the scoring vector; no schema change needed but we'd recommend standardizing tags across your services to get the best hit rate.

[00:02:44] Ethan: on the infra side, any extra network calls for prefetch will be from Redwood's control plane to the serving nodes? i'm worried about cross-vpc egress and extra latency.

[00:02:55] Marcus: prefetch is executed in the same serving path — it's a local call between the router and the worker on the same node or same AZ; there shouldn't be inter-VPC traffic unless you route to different regions. for your private deployment, we'll run the prefetch logic entirely inside your VPC with no egress, that was in the deployment notes.

[00:03:14] Priya: great, confirm that then we are comfortable with compliance as long as it's inside our VPC. also about KMS — are prefixes or KV keys logged in plaintext in any post-mortem logs?

[00:03:27] Alyssa: quick answer: no, we mask keys in logs and we use your KMS for any persisted cache encryption. i'll send the SOC2 + KMS snippet after the call, but Marcus can add the logging config to the config diff.

[00:03:41] Marcus: yes i'll include the log redaction rules, and for the staging run we'll enable verbose metrics so you can see per-prefix cardinality without leaking the actual tokens.

[00:03:54] [00:03:54] Speaker 3: [crosstalk] yeah that would help

[00:04:05] Marcus: back to hit rates — we also evaluated eviction policies. baseline LRU sometimes thrashes for short-lived sessions that have spikes; we prototyped a hybrid eviction (score-aware eviction where low-scoring prefetched keys are evicted first). with that we saw a 6% improved steady-state hit rate for the medium cohort.

[00:04:30] Sara: can you remind me what you mean by "score-aware eviction" in plain English?

[00:04:34] Marcus: basically each cached item has a prefetch score attached; when memory pressure hits, items with low score are the first candidates to evict, rather than strictly by LRU. it's trying to keep the things we think will be reused.

[00:04:50] Priya: okay makes sense. what about prompt reuse? we have been reformatting prompts a lot on the client — adding names and timestamps which break prefix matching. is there a strategy for normalizing prompts so we get higher reuse?

[00:05:06] June: yeah this is a big one. two levers: client-side canonicalization (strip non-semantic noise like timestamps, ephemeral IDs) and server-side coalescing where we maintain canonical prefix buckets — basically normalized prefix -> canonical id mapping. we can do both; canonicalization gives the biggest wins but requires client changes.

[00:05:27] Ethan: client changes are heavy, we prefer a server-side approach if it doesn't change our release schedule. can Redwood do server-side canonicalization non-destructively?

[00:05:34] Marcus: yes, server-side is safe — we compute a hash of normalized prefix and attempt to match to existing keys; it's slower than client-side but no code changes for you. in our tests server-side canonicalization recovered ~18% of broken-prefix cases.

[00:05:50] Marta: any risk of incorrect normalization changing model behavior? like removing tokens that actually carry signal?

[00:05:57] June: we whitelist rules, for example we only strip ISO timestamps and some deterministic IDs; we do not remove natural language tokens. plus we log normalized forms for audit so you can review samples. we also support canarying normalization rules off for a cohort to check quality impact.

[00:06:18] Priya: okay that's helpful. can we see sample normalized traces?

[00:06:22] Marcus: yes we included a short sample in the shared doc — Link: https://redwood.example/decks/metadata-prefetch-samples (we'll also paste the sanitized csv to the shared drive).

[00:06:34] Sara: about costs — prefetching more aggressively raises GPU utilization and could bump monthly costs. what are the expected deltas?

[00:06:42] Marcus: good question. with v1 naive prefetch the expected token-equivalent cost went up ~12% because we were often warming useless keys. with v2 scoring plus selective eviction we estimate net cost change to be neutral to slightly negative (0% to -5%) for cohorts with decent reuse because hit-rate saves downstream tokens. for low reuse cohorts you still see a cost bump, which is why we want cohort-aware thresholds.

[00:07:06] Priya: so bottom line we need to cohort-split production traffic and only enable prefetch for cohorts that show >X reuse. what's our recommended threshold?

[00:07:15] Marcus: we typically recommend enabling for cohorts with historical prefix reuse >20% or where the predicted prefetch score gives an expected return >1.2x cost. for this POC our target is to get aggregate hit rate above 35% in the experimental group while keeping p95 latency under 200ms.

[00:07:33] Sara: latency target seems tight but doable, remind me what's adding to p95?

[00:07:38] June: the extra path is the prefetch scoring and local kv warm call — we optimized that to be non-blocking for generation start when needed, we can request generation to start and prefetch in parallel for low-risk prefixes, only block if predicated latency savings are high. that's where the scoring threshold matters.

[00:07:56] Ethan: how will we measure in the A/B? we need clear metrics so our SREs can sign off.

[00:08:01] Marcus: metrics we'll log per request: was_prefetched (bool), prefetched_keys_count, prefix_hit (bool), latency_total_ms, generation_tokens, cpu_seconds_prefetch. we'll provide a dashboard and per-cohort breakdown. June will produce the dashboard.

[00:08:18] Priya: can you include a metric for "relevance degradation" — like BLEU-ish or our internal QA score in case normalization changes quality?

[00:08:25] June: yes include a quality delta metric — we'll calculate a simple similarity score between baseline and test, and you can run your human QA samples.

[00:08:34] Alyssa: quick security note — Priya asked about logs; we'll redact and provide a hashed sample mapping so you can audit without seeing raw prompts. also for Private deployment we'll use your KMS.

[00:08:47] [00:08:47] Speaker 2: [laughs] ok good

[00:08:55] Marcus: one operational note — we will instrument a kill-switch per-cohort so if p95 latency regresses beyond threshold or quality drops we can auto disable prefetch for that cohort and fall back to baseline.

[00:09:07] Sara: that's required yes.

[00:09:12] Priya: timeline? when can we run the A/B?

[00:09:16] Marcus: if we get the datasets and firewall changes by Friday (2026-01-23) we can spin up the staging A/B on Monday and run for 48 hours, collect metrics, then present results in the follow-up call.

[00:09:29] Ethan: i'll do the firewall, but need the exact ip ranges and port list.

[00:09:33] Alyssa: i'll email the list after this call.

[00:09:36] Marta: regarding prompt coalescing, did you test with our anonymized clinical transcript data? any PII concerns?

[00:09:43] June: yes we ran sanitized traces — we don't store raw unmasked personal data in logs, sanitized only. for on-prem we can align to your retention rules.

[00:09:54] Priya: good. anything else on tuning? eviction windows?

[00:09:58] Marcus: we want to try a slightly longer eviction window for clinician cohort (from 10m to 30m) because reuse is spaced out — that reduced cold misses in our bench. we'll include that as a variant in the A/B.

[00:10:10] Sara: can you describe the variants we'll run?

[00:10:14] Marcus: variant A: baseline (no prefetch). variant B: metadata-prefetch v2 with server-side canonicalization plus score-aware eviction + clinician eviction window 30m for clinician cohort. we'll route 10% of traffic to each variant for the 48h run, stratified by cohort.

[00:10:33] Priya: sounds good. one more ask — when you upload the sanitized samples can you include per-request metadata fields so we can sanity-check mapping?

[00:10:40] Marcus: yes will do.

[00:10:44] Alyssa: ok let's wrap with clear owners: Marcus deploys v2 staging and dashboard, June builds dashboard and similarity score pipeline, Alyssa shares security + ip list, Priya uploads datasets, Ethan opens firewall. Follow-up: 2026-02-04 tentative check-in to review results.

[00:11:05] Priya: thanks everyone, this was useful.

[00:11:09] Sara: thanks

[00:11:12] Marcus: thanks all, will follow up with the config diff.

[00:11:15] Alyssa: meeting end.

Notes: transcript has occasional automatic speaker labeling errors and minor word substitutions due to transcription. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example/decks/metadata-prefetch-samples, https://redwood.example/docs/security-kms, shared drive: /velah/poctests/prefetch_v2.csv

Decisions and agreed experimental plan:
- Run 48h A/B with prefetched v2 vs baseline, target aggregate hit rate >35% and p95 latency <200ms for the experimental group.
- Use cohort-aware enablement; clinician cohort will try longer eviction window (30m).
- Server-side canonicalization enabled for POC; client canonicalization left for future work.
